body.justification: The corrected theorem proves the profile-sensitive \(\inf_h\sup_x\) risk bound for an explicit one-bandwidth anchor-extension estimator.
body.gap: The former \(\sup_x\inf_h\) display was incompatible with one global bandwidth and relied on an unproved varying-radius maximal inequality.
body.consumer: The result supplies a total, measurable, exponent-free estimator whose stochastic penalty is computable from first-half anchor multiplicities.
body.proof_tex:
Let \(\mathcal E_n\) be the event from
\(\mathrm{lem{:}empirical\text{-}packing\text{-}comparison\text{-}same\text{-}radius}\);
uniformly over the declared union of base classes,
\[
 P(\mathcal E_n^c)\leq Cn^{-3}.                                  \tag{T1}
\]
All lists and grids are finite.  The same-radius lemma makes their
source-labeled sorting and the representative map Borel.  Empirical severity
rounding, the ordered greedy scan, first-covering-anchor assignment, finite
maximization over \(G_1(h)\), and smallest-minimizer selection over \(H_n\)
use only finitely many Borel comparisons and arithmetic operations.
Second-half counts and sums are Borel, their zero-count branches are
explicit, and both projections are continuous.  Thus
\((O_1,\ldots,O_n,x)\mapsto\widehat\tau_n(x)\) is Borel.  The supremum loss
is measurable because the construction has finitely many sample-dependent
cells and \(\tau_P\) is continuous by the Lipschitz assumption.  The formula
contains neither \(\kappa\) nor a class label.

For \(h\in H_n\), define
\[
 V_P(h)=\sup_{x\in B}\left[
 Lh+\sigma\sqrt{
 \frac{1+\log\!\left(
 e\{1\vee J_P(h,\min\{1,C_0a_P(x,h)\})\}\right)}
 {na_P(x,h)}}\right],
 \qquad
 \mathcal R_P=\min_{h\in H_n}V_P(h).                              \tag{T2}
\]
The base-mass assumption gives
\(a_P(x,h)\geq c_mh^\kappa>0\), so all divisions and logarithms in
\((\mathrm{T2})\) are well defined.  Choose \(C_0\) larger than the
numerical constant in the severity-net population comparison.

We first compare criteria in the informative regime.  Let \(h\) satisfy
\[
 n_1\inf_{x\in B}a_P(x,h)\geq C\log(en).                          \tag{T3}
\]
On \(\mathcal E_n\), \((\mathrm{P3})\), the exact empirical-pattern identity
at \(x\) and \(g_h(x)\), and the second conclusion of the severity-net lemma
give, for every \(x\),
\[
 a^L(g_h(x),h)\geq\tfrac12a_P(x,h),\qquad
 Z_n(g_h(x),h)
 \leq C\left[1+\log\!\left(
 e\{1\vee J_P(h,\min\{1,C_0a_P(x,h)\})\}\right)\right].           \tag{T4}
\]
Since every \(g\in G_1(h)\) is its own representative, maximizing
\((\mathrm{T4})\) over \(g\) shows that, whenever the right side of
\((\mathrm{T4})\) also makes the admissibility inequalities hold,
\[
 \widehat V(h)\leq C V_P(h).                                     \tag{T5}
\]

Let \(h_\star\) attain the finite minimum in \((\mathrm{T2})\), and put
\(\ell=\log(en)\).  Suppose first that
\[
 \mathcal R_P<c_\star\sigma/\sqrt{\ell},                         \tag{T6}
\]
where \(c_\star>0\) is a sufficiently small numerical constant.
 Write \(z_P(x,h_\star)\) for the logarithmic numerator in
 \((\mathrm{T2})\).  The variance term is at most \(\mathcal R_P\), and
 \(z_P(x,h_\star)\geq1\), so
\[
 \frac{na_P(x,h_\star)}{z_P(x,h_\star)}
 \geq\frac{\sigma^2}{\mathcal R_P^2}
 >c_\star^{-2}\ell,
 \qquad
 na_P(x,h_\star)>c_\star^{-2}\ell
 \quad\text{for every }x\in B.                                  \tag{T7}
\]
Because \(n_1\asymp n_2\asymp n\) for \(n\geq2\), taking \(c_\star\)
small enough makes \((\mathrm{T3})\) and all admissibility inequalities
follow from \((\mathrm{T4})\) and \((\mathrm{T7})\).  Thus
\[
 \widehat V(\widehat h)\leq\widehat V(h_\star)
 \leq C\mathcal R_P
 \quad\text{on }\mathcal E_n.                                   \tag{T8}
\]

For completeness, the complementary regime does not require an unstated
mass assumption.  Suppose
\(\mathcal R_P\geq c_\star\sigma/\sqrt{\ell}\).
For all sufficiently large \(n\), choose \(h_s\in H_n\) with
\[
 (\ell^2/n)^{1/\kappa}\leq h_s<2(\ell^2/n)^{1/\kappa};            \tag{T9}
\]
the compact exponent window and \(h_0>0\) make this possible uniformly.
The base-mass assumption gives
\[
 \inf_xa_P(x,h_s)\geq c_mh_s^\kappa\geq c_m\ell^2/n.             \tag{T10}
\]
On \(\mathcal E_n\), \((\mathrm{P3})\) applies.  Independently of the law,
an \(h_s/2\)-separated subset of the unit-length segment \(B\) has at most
\(1+2/h_s\) points.  Hence
\[
 \max_g Z_n(g,h_s)\leq C\log(e/h_s)\leq C\ell.                   \tag{T11}
\]
Equations \((\mathrm{T10})\)--\((\mathrm{T11})\) make \(h_s\) admissible and
give
\[
 \widehat V(h_s)
 \leq CL(\ell^2/n)^{1/\kappa}+C\sigma/\sqrt{\ell}
 \leq C\sigma/\sqrt{\ell}
 \leq C\mathcal R_P,                                             \tag{T12}
\]
where the penultimate inequality holds uniformly for
\(\kappa\in[2+\epsilon,\bar\kappa]\) once \(n\) is large; its constant may
depend on the fixed ratio \(L/\sigma\).  Therefore \((\mathrm{T8})\) also
holds in this regime.  The finitely many remaining \(n\) are absorbed by
enlarging \(C\): projection bounds the loss by \(4L\), while
\(\mathcal R_P\geq\sigma/\sqrt n\).

On \(\mathcal E_n\), at least one bandwidth is admissible by the preceding
dichotomy, so \(\widehat h\) is the ordinary smallest minimizer and is
\(I_1\)-measurable.  Invoke the conditional conclusion of
\(\mathrm{lem{:}empirical\text{-}severity\text{-}net\text{-}extension}\)
at this single bandwidth.  Equations \((\mathrm{T8})\) and the tower
property yield
\[
 E_P[\|\widehat\tau_n-\tau_P\|_\infty\mathbf1_{\mathcal E_n}]
 \leq C\mathcal R_P.                                              \tag{T13}
\]
On \(\mathcal E_n^c\), both the projected estimator and the target take
values in \([-2L,2L]\), so \((\mathrm{T1})\) bounds the contribution by
\(4LCn^{-3}\).  Since
\(n^{-3}\leq\log^2(en)/n\), combining this with
\((\mathrm{T2})\) and \((\mathrm{T13})\) proves the displayed oracle
inequality.  In particular, the infimum is outside the boundary supremum
because one global bandwidth is used.
